changes: The card's material on squared and cubed factors (touching at a turning point, flattening as it passes through) goes beyond this point's brief and should be removed or limited to the single-factor case.
The card's example and figures use NSW Year 11 framing, so they should be checked against the Victorian Level 10A syllabus wording.
match.reason: The bank card teaches the same idea of sketching a cubic from its factors, the constant term and the sign of the x³ term, but it covers more than this point's brief, so it needs small trimming to fit the Level 10A course.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, Cubic and polynomial graphs, teaches the intercepts and end behaviour but also covers repeated factors (double roots touching, cubed factors flattening), and one of its questions tests a double root, so it goes beyond this brief and needs its own narrower point.

draft.title: Sketching cubics from factors
card: A cubic in factor form, such as \(y = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\), crosses the x-axis where each factor is zero. Here the x-intercepts are \(x = -2\), \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\).
For the y-intercept, put \(x = 0\). Here \(y = (2)(-1)(-3) = 6\), so the curve crosses the y-axis at \((0, 6)\).
The sign of the \(x^{3}\) term sets the ends. If it is positive, the curve starts low on the left and ends high on the right. If it is negative, it starts high and ends low.

Plot the intercepts, then draw a smooth curve through them with the correct ends. This cubic has a positive \(x^{3}\) term, so it rises from the bottom left, passes through all four points and ends high on the right.

4.alt: The cubic \(y = P(x)\) with \(P(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\), rising from the bottom left and ending high on the right. It crosses the x-axis at \((-2, 0)\), \((1, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\), and the y-axis at \((0, 6)\).

draft.remember: Factors give the x-intercepts, \(x = 0\) gives the y-intercept, and the sign of the \(x^{3}\) term gives the ends.

a.q: A cubic is \(y = (x - 4)(x + 1)(x - 2)\). What are its x-intercepts?
a.why: Each factor is zero at an x-intercept: \(x - 4 = 0\) gives \(x = 4\), \(x + 1 = 0\) gives \(x = -1\), and \(x - 2 = 0\) gives \(x = 2\). The tempting option swaps every sign, which is the usual mistake of reading the number in the bracket as the intercept.
a.clue: Solve each bracket equal to zero.

opts: y-intercept \(-6\), ends high on the left and low on the right
y-intercept \(6\), ends high on the left and low on the right
y-intercept \(-6\), ends low on the left and high on the right
y-intercept \(6\), ends low on the left and high on the right
b.why: Put \(x = 0\): \(y = -(1)(-2)(-3) = -6\). Expanding, the \(x^{3}\) term is negative, so the curve starts high on the left and ends low on the right. The tempting option forgets the minus sign out the front when finding the y-intercept.
b.clue: The minus sign in front of the brackets affects the y-intercept and the ends.
